TODDLER 8 · LESSON 14

Garden Bugs & Friends for 2-Year-Olds

Age 2 YearsSubject Nature & TalkClass Toddler 8Duration 3–5 minutes

There is a whole little world wobbling around the garden. Meet it together, one friendly face at a time — a busy bee, a slow snail, a roly-poly that rolls right up.

Nothing to read and nothing to prepare. You say the name, your toddler points or giggles — a moment on a card counts, and the real garden can wait until you step outside.

TOGETHER · LITTLE BUG FACTS

Little bug facts.

Five true things to share while you look — little facts stick when they come with a face.

  • Ladybug

    “Ladybugs are garden helpers — they eat tiny pests off the plants.”

  • Snail

    “A snail’s shell is its house, and it carries it everywhere it goes.”

  • Bee

    “Bees visit flowers to make honey — and help gardens grow.”

  • Firefly

    “A firefly makes its own light so it can glow at night.”

  • Earthworm

    “Earthworms wiggle through the soil and keep it cozy for roots.”

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the garden cards together.

The twenty garden cards print two to a page. Printed, cut and named, they turn the next walk outside into the class’s final page.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty, two to a page. Cut them out together, saying each garden friend’s name.

  2. 02

    Name and greet

    Hold up a card and greet the friend — “hello, bee!”. Naming warmly is how words stick at two.

  3. 03

    Move like them

    Wiggle like a worm, flutter like a butterfly, roll like a roly-poly. Bodies remember what ears forget.

  4. 04

    Take it outside

    Carry two or three cards on the next walk and find their real twins. We look, we talk, and the bugs stay where they live.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Garden hunt.

Take the names outside — or to a window, a book or a video if the garden is far away.

Try one today

  • Look for a bee visiting a flower.
  • Count the snails after it rains.
  • Find a bird and say hello to it.
  • Wiggle like a worm, then hop like a grasshopper.
  • Peek under a stone for a roly-poly — look, then gently roll it back.

One found friend is a complete hunt. If nothing turns up, the squirrel outside the window counts too.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Follow your toddler’s favourites. If they want the snail five times in a row, the snail five times in a row it is — repetition is how little ones learn.

Sounds before facts. Buzzing, hopping and wiggling teach the names better than any explanation, so be as silly as your toddler needs you to be.

Bring the class outside when you can. A found ladybug, a heard cricket or a visiting bird turns every name on these cards into something real.

Age ranges are a guide. Go at your child’s pace.

    Bee — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts the garden with its busiest worker: your toddler learns the word bee, makes the buzzy sound, and meets the golden rule that holds the whole set together — eyes do the visiting, hands stay down.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A bee is a small flying insect with yellow and black stripes that visits flowers to gather pollen and make honey. Bees spend the whole day travelling from bloom to bloom — the garden’s own delivery service.

    What does it mean?

    The bee is the loudest hello in the garden and usually the first bug a toddler can already point at. Naming it properly turns a random buzz into a friend greeted by name — and the bee carries the set’s most important rule on its stripes.

    What does the child need to know?

    Two things matter: bees say bzzz and visit flowers all day long, and we watch them without touching. Bees are busy workers, not pettable pets — calm eyes and down-held hands are how we say hello.

    Why this matters

    Look-don’t-grab is easiest to learn from a bee, because the reason is built into everyday life: everyone already treats bees with respect. Your toddler practises the rule exactly where the whole family already follows it.

    What it teaches

    First-insect vocabulary, sound imitation (bzzz is a lifelong favourite), watching-without-touching — genuine impulse practice — and the early idea that living things have jobs to do.

    Words to learn

    beebuzzflowersstripeshoneygentle

    Say this to your child

    “"Here is the bee! Bzzz... can you say bzzz? The bee wears stripes and it loves flowers. When we see a real bee, we stand still like trees and watch — no grabbing, no squealing. Bees are busy, and our job is to watch them work."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say bee slowly, twice — then add a long buzzy bzzz together, so the word arrives with its sound.
    2. Ask your toddler to find the bee’s smile and trace its stripes with one finger — the picture study that two-year-olds do best.
    3. Make your hand a little bee and fly it around the room, touching down softly on cushions and shoulders — soft landings only, bees are careful pilots.
    4. Look out of a window at any flowers and whisper: is a bee visiting right now? Maybe, maybe not — the looking is the game.
    5. End with the rule in toddler words: bees are watch-friends. We look, we buzz, and our hands stay down by our sides.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say bee together and give the card a big buzzy bzzz. The bee on this card is friendly and smiling — ask your toddler to find its smile and point at the stripes. Pointing is how two-year-olds study a picture.

    Ask your child

    "What does the bee say?" "Can you find the stripes?" "Where does the bee go all day?" "Do our hands touch the bee, or stay down?" — answered with a buzz, a point and a solemn little nod.

    What your child can say or do

    "Bzzz!" delivered at full volume, hand-bees circling your head at breakfast, and bees pointed out in books, on rugs, out of prams. Some toddlers will freeze into their best statue pose at the first real buzz — the rule already working.

    Out in the real world

    Bees appear wherever flowers do — window boxes, balconies, the lawn, the herb pot on the sill. Every real buzz is a rerun: whisper bee, keep feet still, watch it work, wave it goodbye.

    Try it together

    Bumble landing: your toddler flies around as the bee while you hold up a cushion-flower. Touching down softly on the flower scores a cheer; bumpy crashes get a gentle reminder that careful bees make the best honey.

    Understanding check

    Next time a bee flies past outside, watch the hands: if they stay down and the mouth whispers bee, the lesson landed — watching replaced grabbing, which was the whole point.

    Parent tips

    Practise the statue pose on the card first, when no bee is anywhere near — calm is rehearsed best in peacetime. Keep sessions short: one buzz, one point, one rule, done.

    Staying safe

    Bees sting when they feel squashed or trapped, so the looking happens from a little way back and hands stay far away. If one lands close by, still feet and a quiet voice until it lifts off — and a grown-up guides the moment, never a swatting hand.

    This lesson pairs with the Bee flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    Butterfly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes the prettiest card a whole-body game: your toddler becomes a butterfly, flapping slow and gentle, then learns the watching rule — a butterfly’s wings belong to the air, not to our hands.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A butterfly is an insect with two pairs of big painted wings that flap slowly from flower to flower. It lands to sip nectar, rests with its wings open, and flies off the moment anything moves too fast.

    What does it mean?

    Butterflies hand a two-year-old the perfect movement word: flutter. The flap is slow, the mood is calm, and the animal is far too quick and delicate to hold — which is exactly why the lesson works on gentleness.

    What does the child need to know?

    Butterflies flap slowly and love flowers, and they are look-at friends: chasing only sends them away. Hands stay down; the wings are prettiest in the air where they belong.

    Why this matters

    A creature that leaves when chased teaches cause and effect more kindly than any lecture: quick hands mean a gone butterfly, still hands mean it stays. The lesson teaches self-control with a living, flying reward.

    What it teaches

    Slow-and-gentle body control (the crossed-wing flap is surprisingly tricky), vocabulary for wings and flowers, watching practice at garden speed, and the earliest what-happens-if reasoning.

    Words to learn

    butterflyflutterwingsflowerssoftslow

    Say this to your child

    “"A butterfly! Big painted wings — flap, flap, slowly, slowly. Butterflies love flowers and take their time. When we see one, we walk soft and watch with our eyes. Our hands stay down, and the butterfly stays with us a little longer."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say butterfly — a big, beautiful mouthful, so say it slowly and let your toddler try the syllables.
    2. Lift both arms overhead, cross them at the wrists, and flap slowly — a butterfly’s own unhurried flutter — and let your toddler copy.
    3. Flutter around one cushion together: slow wings find flowers, fast wings scare them away. The speed is the lesson.
    4. Whisper the story: butterflies sip from flowers, rest a while, then fly off — so we tiptoe past and let them get on with it.
    5. Finish with the rule, warm and short: butterflies are look-at friends. We flap like them, we watch them, and our hands stay empty.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say butterfly together, then make slow crossed-arm wings. The butterfly on this card has orange and black wings — ask your toddler which colour shows the most, and flap once for each colour they can find.

    Ask your child

    "What do the butterfly’s wings look like?" "Can you flutter slowly?" "Where does the butterfly like to rest?" "Do we catch the butterfly, or watch it?" — answered with a flap, a whisper and a proud head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Fly!" with crossed-arm flaps at the window, butterflies discovered in every second picture book, and the first real sighting met with a hush instead of a dash — the gentleness training already showing.

    Out in the real world

    Butterflies drift through gardens, parks and balconies on sunny days, resting on petals and fences. Each one is a rerun: name it, flap once, watch it sip, and let it drift off without a single grabbed handful.

    Try it together

    Flower to flower: scatter a few paper flowers on the floor and flutter from one to the next, resting at each with wings open — slow, calm, and the finest quiet-time game in the set.

    Understanding check

    Ask for the butterfly move tomorrow: crossed arms and a slow flap means the word has grown wings. If your toddler whispers instead of shouting at a real one, the gentleness has landed too.

    Parent tips

    Flap slowly yourself — your pace sets your toddler’s. If a real butterfly startles and darts away, narrate the happy ending: it flew home. Chasing is not a failure; it is simply the next chance to practise still hands.

    Staying safe

    Butterfly wings are covered in tiny dust-fine scales that fingers rub off, so catching squeezes the colour right off them — and garden flowers may host other bugs too. Watching from a small distance keeps both the butterfly and the toddler clean.

    This lesson pairs with the Butterfly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    Ladybug — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the garden’s tiniest celebrity into a pointing-and-counting game: your toddler finds the spots, counts as far as the mood holds, and hears the lovely secret that ladybugs look after the flowers.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A ladybug is a very small, round beetle with a red shell and black spots. It crawls slowly over leaves and stems, eating tiny bugs that would otherwise nibble the garden — a small friend with a big job.

    What does it mean?

    The ladybug matches a toddler’s own scale: little, round, red and friendly. Pointing at its spots is often a two-year-old’s very first purposeful counting — real pointing, real numbers, one tiny beetle.

    What does the child need to know?

    The ladybug is red with spots and crawls on leaves, and it helps the flowers by eating pests. It is a look-at friend too — small things are exactly the things fingers want to poke, so hands stay gentle and down.

    Why this matters

    Counting spots on a card is counting without pressure: any number reached is a win, and the same beetle offers a fresh total every time. The helper story plants the first seed of caring for the garden.

    What it teaches

    Early counting with real pointing, colour naming (red and black), fine-motor pointing at tiny targets, and the first this-creature-has-a-job idea, planted small.

    Words to learn

    ladybugspotsredtinycountgentle

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — a ladybug! Red and round with little black spots. Can you point to a spot? One... two! The ladybug munches the bugs that nibble the leaves, so the flowers say thank you. We watch our tiny friend and keep our big fingers to ourselves."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say ladybug — then let your toddler find it: where is the little red friend sitting?
    2. Hunt the spots together: point to one, then another, saying one, two for as long as the counting mood holds — any total is a triumph.
    3. Draw a big ladybug on paper and let your toddler add the dots with a finger dipped in paint or a fat crayon — the spottier the better.
    4. Tell the helper story in one line: the ladybug eats the tiny bugs that nibble the leaves, so the flowers say thank you.
    5. End with the rule: the ladybug is so small that our big fingers stay far away — we look, we count, and it crawls on its way.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the ladybug together and say its long, lovely name. This ladybug is red with spots — ask your toddler to point at each spot they can find, and count along for as long as the pointing stays happy.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the ladybug?" "What colour is it?" "Can you find a spot?" "Do our fingers touch the tiny ladybug, or stay far away?" — answered with points, a colour word and a careful little head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ladybug!" shouted at anything red and round, spots pointed out on every page from now on, and thumbs painted with dots at craft time. Some toddlers will lower one careful finger towards a real ladybug — the moment to open your palm and redirect to looking.

    Out in the real world

    Ladybugs land on leaves, walls and pram hoods all summer. Each one is a rerun: whisper the name, point out the spots you can see, say thank you for helping the flowers, and let it crawl off untouched.

    Try it together

    Spot-sticker ladybug: draw a big red circle, then hand your toddler black stickers or crayon dots to place wherever spots belong. Peeling and pressing is real fine-motor work wearing a ladybug costume.

    Understanding check

    Show any red-dotted picture tomorrow and ask what it is: a quick ladybug means the word and the shape have bonded. Then ask what ladybugs do all day — munching the leaf-nibblers is the answer worth waiting for.

    Parent tips

    Count to whatever number the day allows: two spots today, five next week — the pointing matters more than the total. Keep paint dots big and taste-safe, because fingers wander to mouths at two.

    Staying safe

    A ladybug is fingernail-small, so the looking happens with hands down and eyes close. After any garden or paint session, wash little hands — and nothing from the garden, spots or leaves or bugs, ever goes near a mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Ladybug flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    Snail — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is a race to be last: your toddler learns the word snail, crawls across the room at the world’s slowest speed, and meets the garden friend that takes its home along everywhere it goes.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A snail is a small, soft creature with a spiral shell on its back that moves — very, very slowly — on one slim foot. Snails come out when the air is damp, after rain or overnight, and munch leaves as they go.

    What does it mean?

    Slow is a genuinely difficult speed for a two-year-old, and the snail makes it a game instead of a command. The shell-house story gives the slowness a reason: the snail carries everything it owns, so of course it takes its time.

    What does the child need to know?

    Snails are slow and carry spiral shells, and damp days bring them out. We watch them without touching — and after any snail encounter, hands go straight to the sink.

    Why this matters

    Crawling slowly builds body control that crawling fast never touches, and the waiting teaches patience with a living example: the snail always arrives, just later. Damp-day snail hunts turn rainy weather into an event.

    What it teaches

    Slow-motion body control, a first spiral shape found in the wild, weather words (rain, damp, wet), and gentle observation — following one small creature’s whole journey across a step.

    Words to learn

    snailslowshellrainhousewatch

    Say this to your child

    “"A snail! Slow, slow, slow — see its shell-house riding on its back? It never hurries anywhere. After rain, snails come out for a walk. We watch them crawl, we never touch, and then we wash our hands like big kids."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say snail — then ask where its house is: right there on its back, taken along everywhere.
    2. Trace the shell’s round curl on the card with one finger, round and round and in — a spiral is a lovely new shape.
    3. Crawl across the rug at snail speed together: the rule is that nobody may hurry, and the slowest crawler wins the giggle.
    4. After rain, check a wall or a plant pot for a real snail and watch it travel at its own pace — one whole minute is a long, marvellous time.
    5. End with the routine: we looked at the snail, so now we walk inside and wash our hands — snails are watched, never pocketed.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say snail together and find the shell — this snail has a brown shell and a smile. Trace the curl with one finger, round and round, and ask whether the snail looks like it is going anywhere in a hurry.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the snail’s house?" "Can you crawl slowly, slowly?" "When do snails come out?" "Do we touch the snail or watch it?" — answered with a point, a crawl and a slow-motion grin.

    What your child can say or do

    "Slowwww snail!" announced at every pace slower than usual, snails spotted on pavements and flowerpots after rain, and a crawl across the kitchen that takes genuinely forever — the point of the whole game.

    Out in the real world

    Rainy days turn every pavement and garden wall into a snail safari. Each find is a rerun: crouch, whisper snail, watch the neck stretch, and leave it exactly where it was heading.

    Try it together

    Snail race — in reverse: mark a start and a finish cushion, and the winner is whoever takes the longest to cross. Slow motion, silly faces, and the best self-control workout disguised as a race.

    Understanding check

    Say slow out of nowhere tomorrow and watch what happens: a deliberate, exaggerated crawl means the snail left its word behind — the speed and the animal are glued together.

    Parent tips

    Practise the hand-washing line with a happy voice every single time — the routine matters more than the snail. If rain never comes, a watering can on the same flowerpot makes a fine pretend-damp morning.

    Staying safe

    Snails trail through soil, leaves and whatever the garden has hosted, so looking is eyes-only and hands get washed straight after garden play. Nothing from the garden — snail, leaf or shell — ever goes near a mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Snail flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    Ant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson finds the smallest card in the set and makes it the busiest: your toddler marches like an ant, follows a real line with their eyes, and learns that ants are always on their way somewhere important.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    An ant is a very small insect with six legs that walks in long lines with its many friends, carrying crumbs and seeds far bigger than itself. Ants are always going somewhere — usually home.

    What does it mean?

    Ants are the first teamwork a toddler can actually see: a whole line of tiny workers, all heading the same way. The marching game puts your child inside that line, and the watching rule keeps the real workers unbothered.

    What does the child need to know?

    Ants are tiny and march in long lines, and they are heading home with food. We follow a line with our eyes — never fingers — because a bothered ant can nip, and busy workers deserve to get home.

    Why this matters

    Following an ant line with the eyes is real focus training: the line moves, turns and disappears, and your toddler’s attention follows it. The picnic rule teaches the boundary kindly — food is for people, ants have their own plan.

    What it teaches

    Visual tracking of a moving line, marching and carrying (real heavy-work play), the concept of many-and-small, and early respect for creatures with their own business.

    Words to learn

    antmarchlinetinyhomewatch

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — tiny ants, all in a line! They are carrying their food home, just like you carry your cup. March, march, little ant! When we see real ants, we stand still and watch with our eyes. Busy ants go home; our hands stay up here."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say ant — then hold it low and ask where the tiny ant might be going today.
    2. March like an ant together: small quick steps, arms swinging, maybe carrying a toy crumb — a line of one is still a line.
    3. Lay a trail of toy ants (or buttons) across the rug and follow it, narrating left, right, over, around — the trail is the game.
    4. At a real picnic or on the pavement, find an ant line and watch it with still bodies: where do they all lead? Home, always home.
    5. End with the rule, kindly: ants have their own work, so we watch with our eyes and our snacks stay on our plate.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the small ant on this card together and say ant. Ask where it might be heading, then march on the spot like a tiny worker — the picture study at ant scale is all in the pointing.

    Ask your child

    "Where are the ants marching?" "Can you march like an ant?" "Are ants big or tiny?" "Do our fingers chase the ants, or do our eyes?" — answered with marching, the word tiny and pointing fingers.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ants going home!" narrated at every pavement crack, marching lines through the kitchen with teddy crumbs, and ants located on every walk within seconds — the small world now officially open for business.

    Out in the real world

    Ant lines cross pavements, garden paths and picnic blankets all summer. Each one is a rerun: crouch, follow with the eyes, whisper where-are-they-going, and leave the line to its work.

    Try it together

    Ant crumb relay: your toddler carries one small toy crumb from the rug to a basket, over and over, like a worker on the line. Repetitive hauling is exactly what ant bodies do — and exactly what toddler bodies love.

    Understanding check

    Watch the next real ant line: if your toddler crouches to watch instead of stomping, the lesson landed — the eyes took over from the feet, which was always the plan.

    Parent tips

    Follow one line as far as it goes; the destination matters more than the count. Keep picnic boundaries warm and firm — ants are not chased off, they are simply watched from the blanket.

    Staying safe

    An ant nips when it is bothered, so the watching is strictly eyes-only with hands folded or held. Food stays with people and gets cleared up after eating — a tidy picnic is the kindest thing anyone can do for ants and toddlers alike.

    This lesson pairs with the Ant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).
