    Caterpillar — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gets low and wiggly: your toddler inches across the rug like a caterpillar, munches through an imaginary garden, and hears the astonishing news that this slow green friend turns into the butterfly card.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A caterpillar is a long, soft, many-legged crawler that spends its whole day eating leaves and growing. One day — a bit like magic, but really just growing up — it becomes a butterfly.

    What does it mean?

    The caterpillar is the garden’s appetite champion, and toddlers respect appetite. The inch-and-scrunch movement is genuinely funny to do, and the butterfly promise gives the card a secret that keeps it rewatchable for months.

    What does the child need to know?

    Caterpillars inch along and munch leaves, and every one is a butterfly-in-waiting. They are look-at friends from a little distance — some kinds carry prickly fuzz, so the rule covers them all: eyes only.

    Why this matters

    The inchworm move builds coordination from shoulders to hips in a way nothing else does, and the grow-and-change story is a toddler’s first transformation — the same story they will meet in every butterfly book from now on.

    What it teaches

    Sequenced movement (reach, scrunch, reach), the munch-and-chew pretending that feeds language, transformation as a concept, and gentle observation of very small travellers.

    Words to learn

    caterpillarinchmunchleavesgreenbutterfly

    Say this to your child

    “"A caterpillar! Long and green and always munching. Can you inch the way it does? Reach... scrunch... reach... And guess what — one day this little friend grows wings and becomes a butterfly! We watch caterpillars with our eyes and let them munch."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say caterpillar — a long word, so stretch it out and let your toddler feel all its syllables.
    2. Get down and inch across the rug together: reach forward with the hands, then tuck the legs in — reach, scrunch, reach, scrunch.
    3. Munch through the garden: each cushion or rug corner is a leaf, and every caterpillar stops to munch it down, bite by bite.
    4. Whisper the secret: this little crawler is growing wings inside its dreams — one day, butterfly. Bring the butterfly card over and let the two meet.
    5. End with the rule: caterpillars are look-at friends from a little way off — fuzz and all, our hands stay back.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say caterpillar together and meet the green crawler on the card. Ask your toddler to trace its long body with one finger from head to tail, then inch two fingers along the card like a tiny crawler.

    Ask your child

    "What does the caterpillar eat?" "Can you inch like a caterpillar?" "What will it grow into?" "Do we touch the caterpillar, or watch from far away?" — answered with a munch, an inch and a whispered butterfly.

    What your child can say or do

    "Munch munch!" announced at every meal, inchworm races across the living room, and caterpillars inspected solemnly in books with the announcement growing wings — the transformation story already retold in toddler.

    Out in the real world

    Caterpillars cruise along leaves, walls and paths in spring and summer. Each find is a rerun: crouch at a polite distance, whisper the name, watch it inch, and leave it to its lunch.

    Try it together

    Leaf munch trail: lay a trail of green paper leaves across the rug and inch-munch from leaf to leaf, one bite per leaf. Add the butterfly ending: wrap up in a blanket, count to three, and burst out flapping.

    Understanding check

    Ask what a caterpillar becomes: a delighted butterfly is the whole harvest. If the inch-and-scrunch crawl shows up unasked at playtime, the movement landed too — lesson complete.

    Parent tips

    Join the inching every time; the move is funnier with a grown-up doing it badly. Keep the transformation simple — growing wings inside is plenty of magic for two, no need for the full cocoon science yet.

    Staying safe

    Some caterpillars carry irritating fuzz that can sting bare skin, so every caterpillar is watched from a little distance, never touched. Hands get washed after garden play, and leaves stay on the plant — not anywhere near a mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Caterpillar flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Dragonfly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the fastest card at three speeds: your toddler hovers like a dragonfly, darts once, then freezes mid-air — and lands gently on a lily pad, just the way the real flyer does.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A dragonfly is a long, thin insect with four glittering wings that zips over ponds and streams, hovers in one spot, then darts off after smaller bugs. It is one of the best flyers in the whole garden.

    What does it mean?

    Hover-dart-freeze is a toddler movement masterpiece: three speeds in one body, ending in the dramatic mid-air stop. And the pond setting makes it the perfect card for practising water-safety rules in play form.

    What does the child need to know?

    Dragonflies zoom and hover near water, and they are look-at friends like everyone in the set. Near any real pond or stream, a grown-up holds the hand — the wings stay in the air game, well away from the water’s edge.

    Why this matters

    The freeze is the secret prize: stopping mid-action is real impulse control, dressed as a dragonfly trick. Pairing it with the pond rule means the quickest card in the set quietly teaches its calmest lesson.

    What it teaches

    Speed switching (hover, dart, freeze), balance on soft landings, pond-and-water vocabulary, and the safety habit of hand-holding near water, rehearsed long before it is ever needed.

    Words to learn

    dragonflywingszoomfreezepondgentle

    Say this to your child

    “"Zoom! A dragonfly — four shiny wings! Can you hover? Now dart... and freeze, right in the air, like this! Dragonflies fly over ponds, and ponds mean we hold a grown-up’s hand. Soft wings, soft landings, still feet by the water."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say dragonfly — then point out the wings: this flyer wears a shiny set of them.
    2. Be a dragonfly together: arms out wide, hover in one spot, then dart two steps sideways — and freeze! Mid-air, mid-word, everywhere.
    3. Spread cushions as lily pads and fly from pad to pad, touching down softly each time — a dragonfly lands like a feather.
    4. Tell the water story simply: real dragonflies live by ponds, and ponds are grown-up-hand places — we visit with fingers linked.
    5. End with three speeds on request: hover... dart... freeze! Then one last feather landing to finish.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say dragonfly together and find the shiny wings on the card — this dragonfly has wings that glint. Ask your toddler to flap their own wings once, then make them go still as the card.

    Ask your child

    "What does the dragonfly do?" "Can you hover and freeze?" "Where do dragonflies fly — over what?" "What do our hands do near a pond?" — answered with a zoom, a freeze and a linked-hand gesture.

    What your child can say or do

    "Zoom, freeze!" played down corridors at top speed and full stop, dragonflies announced at every puddle and pond, and mid-air freezes held with tremendous seriousness — the stop is the trophy move.

    Out in the real world

    Dragonflies patrol ponds, canals and damp meadows all summer, often resting on reeds and railings. Each sighting is a rerun: hover-watch quietly, then move on with feet safe and hand held near water.

    Try it together

    Mid-air statues: dance and dart while a song plays, then freeze like a hovering dragonfly when it stops — wings out, one foot up if brave. The stopping is the game, and the giggles are the reward.

    Understanding check

    Call freeze during ordinary play tomorrow: an instant statue means the dragonfly left its trick behind — self-control arrived on four glittering wings, exactly as designed.

    Parent tips

    Practise the freeze before the zoom — stopping on cue is the skill worth polishing. Mention the hand-holding rule cheerfully at bath time too; water rules work best when they are rehearsed everywhere.

    Staying safe

    Real dragonflies live at the water’s edge, so pond and stream visits happen hand-in-hand with a grown-up and never at a run. Dragonflies themselves are harmless — looked at, never caught, and left to their buzzing.

    This lesson pairs with the Dragonfly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Grasshopper — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is pure launch power: your toddler crouches like the grasshopper on the card, counts down with you, and jumps — then finds out that grasshoppers leap much farther than their own size, and so can legs that practise.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A grasshopper is a green insect with long, strong back legs made for jumping. It hides down in grass and tall plants, then leaps away in one big bound when anything comes near — nobody else in the garden jumps further.

    What does it mean?

    The grasshopper is the set’s jumping card, and jumping is what two-year-old legs dream about. The countdown before each leap adds the best bit: waiting one, two, three makes the jump itself twice as big.

    What does the child need to know?

    Grasshoppers crouch and leap, and they live down in the grass. We jump on rugs and mats, not hard floors — and in real grass we take big careful steps first, because hiding friends do not like being stepped on.

    Why this matters

    Countdown-then-jump builds listening, waiting and explosive movement in one game, and measuring jumps with steps is the gentlest first maths: how far did MY leap go? Bodies learn; numbers sneak in behind.

    What it teaches

    Powerful crouch-and-jump mechanics, counting down as impulse control, early measuring and comparing, and care for small hidden things — watching the ground as well as the sky.

    Words to learn

    grasshopperjumpcrouchlegsgrassready

    Say this to your child

    “"Grasshopper! Look how it crouches... ready, set — JUMP! Grasshoppers have big strong legs and they hide down in the grass. We jump on the rug, and in the garden we watch our feet. One, two, three — launch!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say grasshopper — then crouch down low yourself, knees bent, ready: your shape teaches first.
    2. Count down together — one, two, three — then jump! Land, laugh, and crouch again for the next launch.
    3. Measure the jumps: heel-to-toe steps from take-off to landing, counted out loud. Grasshoppers leap many times their own length — can you?
    4. Tell the hiding story: grasshoppers live down in the grass, so in real grass we take big careful steps and walk first, jump later.
    5. End with the biggest jump of the day — then a tiny grasshopper crouch, still and quiet, hiding just like the card.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say grasshopper together and find the long back legs on the card — this grasshopper is green and ready to jump. Crouch like it, hold for a breath, then do one big jump right there on the rug.

    Ask your child

    "How does the grasshopper jump — big or small?" "Can you crouch and leap?" "Where does the grasshopper hide?" "In the grass, do we run or watch our feet?" — answered with a crouch, a leap and careful little steps.

    What your child can say or do

    "One, two, three, JUMP!" chanted at sofas, beds and every puddle-adjacent paving stone, jumps measured against grown-up feet all afternoon, and grasshoppers imagined springing from every patch of long grass.

    Out in the real world

    Grasshoppers spring out of long grass, meadows and hedge edges all summer — usually seen only as a flash of green. Each flash is a rerun: freeze, whisper grasshopper, watch where it landed, and step carefully.

    Try it together

    Lily-pad jumping course: cushions or paper pads laid out across the rug, crouch and leap from pad to pad, counting each launch. Land on the pads, not the floor — the aiming is half the exercise.

    Understanding check

    Set up a countdown tomorrow with no card in sight: one, two, three — if a big jump arrives on cue, the legs learned the lesson as well as the ears did.

    Parent tips

    Jump on soft surfaces only, and jump with your toddler — your leap sets the standard and your landing shows the technique. Keep the measuring silly and short; three heel-to-toe steps is a whole adventure.

    Staying safe

    All jumping happens on rugs, mats or grass, never tiles or hard floors, and the jump zone gets cleared of furniture first. In real long grass, walkers watch for stones and holes — and for the tiny hidden friends who were there first.

    This lesson pairs with the Grasshopper flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Beetle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson goes on the set’s gentlest expedition: your toddler meets the round shiny beetle on the card, then joins a real flowerpot-lift — grown-up hands lifting, toddler eyes discovering, roof back on carefully at the end.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A beetle is a small insect with a hard, shiny shell over its wings, and there are more kinds of beetle than almost any other creature. This one trundles along on six legs, tucking under stones, pots and logs by day.

    What does it mean?

    The beetle card is the doorway to the hidden world: the dark, damp addresses under pots and stones where small creatures wait. Your toddler learns that lifting a stone is opening a door — and doors get closed again.

    What does the child need to know?

    Beetles are round and shiny and like dark, damp corners. Only grown-ups do the lifting, everybody looks quickly and kindly, and the stone or pot always goes back — that is somebody’s roof, and roof-back is the whole game.

    Why this matters

    Peek-under-the-pot is genuine discovery science: a guess, a look, and a gentle finish. The put-it-back rule teaches respect for other creatures’ homes long before any pet or nature table arrives.

    What it teaches

    Turn-taking (grown-up lifts, child looks), observation of small shiny things, the hidden-world idea, and early conservation manners — leaving places exactly as found.

    Words to learn

    beetleshellshinystonegentleroof

    Say this to your child

    “"A beetle! Round and shiny with a hard little shell. Beetles like dark, cosy places under stones and pots. Shall we look under one? Grown-up lifts, we look with our eyes... and back goes the roof, so our beetle friend stays snug."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say beetle — then trace the round shell with one finger: shiny, smooth, like a little helmet.
    2. Walk like a beetle together: low, slow and steady, arms tucked — trundling is the speed of the day.
    3. Take the card to the garden and choose one flowerpot with your toddler: who might live underneath? Guess first.
    4. Grown-up lifts the pot, toddler looks with still hands: a beetle, a worm, woodlice — hello! Quick look, quiet voices.
    5. Put the roof back gently together, and say the golden line: we always put the house back. That is the beetle’s whole lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say beetle together, then hunt the card: where is the round, shiny one hiding? Ask your toddler to rub a fingertip gently over the picture to feel how shiny it looks, then trundle two fingers along the card like a little beetle.

    Ask your child

    "Where does the beetle like to hide?" "Who lifts the pot — you or me?" "What did we see underneath?" "What do we do with the stone afterwards?" — answered with points, a solemn me-or-you and the proud word back.

    What your child can say or do

    "Roof back on!" reported after every pot-lift, beetles located under every rock and log from then on, and trundle-walking adopted as regular playground transport — the hidden world now has a doorman.

    Out in the real world

    Beetles trundle through gardens, parks and windowsills all year, most often glimpsed under pots, logs and leaves. Every find is a rerun: look, admire the shine, and lower the roof gently before walking on.

    Try it together

    Under-the-cup peek: hide a toy beetle under one of two cups and let your toddler lift each one — beetle or no beetle? Small thrills, tidy finish, and every cup goes back exactly where it was.

    Understanding check

    Next garden visit, watch the ending, not the beginning: a pot put back without being asked means the lesson landed — the respect part arrived, which was the hard-won half.

    Parent tips

    Keep pot-lifting to one or two pots per visit; one good discovery beats a flipped garden. Do the guessing out loud before each lift — imagination does half of the walking to the flowerbed.

    Staying safe

    Lifting is strictly grown-up work — pots are heavy, edges are rough, and the residents underneath can surprise everyone. After any soil or stone play, hands go to the sink, and nothing from underneath a pot goes anywhere near a mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Beetle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Spider — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the card that makes grown-ups jump and hands it to your toddler as a game: eight legs to wiggle, a web to weave from wool, and one unshakable rule — real spiders are watched with calm eyes and never touched.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A spider is a small creature with eight legs that spins a web from its own silky thread. The web catches breakfast, the spider sits and waits, and the whole contraption is rebuilt almost every day.

    What does it mean?

    A spider met on a card first is a spider met calmly: the picture does the introducing, the wool web does the explaining, and by the time a real one appears, watching is already the family habit.

    What does the child need to know?

    Spiders have eight legs and weave webs, and they are strictly look-at friends — the calmest rule in the set. Webs are admired, never poked, and real spiders stay wherever they built their homes.

    Why this matters

    Calm comes from knowing the job: a spider is not lurking, it is working — spinning, waiting, tidying up. A toddler who understands the web sees a worker, not a monster, and the eight-legged fright shrinks to eight-legged interest.

    What it teaches

    Counting to eight with real wiggles, weaving and threading as fine-motor work, fear met gently through play, and the habit of quiet observation around things that startle.

    Words to learn

    spiderweblegsspinsilkcalm

    Say this to your child

    “"A spider! Eight legs — count them with your fingers: wiggle, wiggle, all eight! Spiders spin webs to catch their dinner. When we see a real web, we look with our eyes and keep our hands down. The spider is busy; we are its quiet visitors."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say spider — then wiggle eight fingers at each other like eight busy legs: four each, all wiggling.
    2. Count the legs out loud together, one wiggle per leg — eight is a very satisfying number to reach with hands.
    3. Weave a web: loop wool or string across the backs of two chairs, in and over, while your toddler watches and helps hold — then flick pom-pom flies into it for the spider to catch.
    4. Explain the job simply: the spider spins its web, waits, and catches its own dinner — nobody brings it a plate.
    5. End with the rule, calm as anything: real spiders are look-at friends. Webs stay un-poked, spiders stay in their homes, and our hands stay in ours.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say spider together and wiggle eight finger-legs. Ask your toddler to find a leg on the card and wiggle just that one — then hold all ten toddler fingers still as a resting spider, which is harder and funnier than it sounds.

    Ask your child

    "How many legs does the spider have?" "What does it spin?" "Do our fingers touch the web, or do our eyes do the looking?" "Where does the spider live?" — answered with wiggles, a spinning motion and gentle pointing.

    What your child can say or do

    Eight wiggling fingers at the dinner table, wool webs requested daily, and spiders reported calmly from the garden: "spider working!" — the startle replaced by interest, which was the whole quiet plan.

    Out in the real world

    Webs appear on hedges, corners and railings, loveliest with morning dew strung across them. Each one is a rerun: crouch, admire the threads, look for the weaver, and walk on without touching a single strand.

    Try it together

    Web rescue: toss small pom-poms into your wool web, and your toddler plucks them free — careful fingers, one at a time, like a very kind spider tidying up. Unpicking is as absorbing as weaving.

    Understanding check

    Meet a real web tomorrow and watch the hands: still, or reaching? Still hands and a whispered spider mean the calm took — the card did its introducing exactly as planned.

    Parent tips

    If webs make you jumpy, borrow the calm anyway — your face is the lesson. Keep the wool web up for days; coming back to it daily is what turns a game into understanding.

    Staying safe

    Some spiders bite when squeezed, and webs stick to little fingers, so real webs and real spiders are admired from a small distance with hands down. The wool-and-chairs web hands your toddler the whole story with zero eight-legged surprises.

    This lesson pairs with the Spider flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Moth — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the garden’s night shift: your toddler learns that some friends wake up at bedtime, flutters around the room on soft brown wings, and watches a lit porch from inside — where the moths come to visit, and no hands go out.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A moth is a soft-winged cousin of the butterfly that flies at night. Moths flutter around lamps and porch lights after dark, bump gently along, and rest in the day with their wings spread wide.

    What does it mean?

    The moth introduces night as a working time — the garden has an evening crew. For a two-year-old at bedtime, that idea is delicious: somewhere out there, soft wings are just clocking in.

    What does the child need to know?

    Moths have soft wings and love lamps at night, and they are watch-from-inside friends: the light stays on, the window stays shut, and the fluttering happens with arms, never with hands.

    Why this matters

    Night-watching from a window gives toddlers a safe, thrilling view into the dark — and turns bedtime from an ending into a handover: we sleep, the moths work. The soft-wing flutter also calms a busy body beautifully.

    What it teaches

    Day-and-night as a first sorting idea, slow gentle movement (the softest flapping in the set), watching patience at a window, and cosy associations that help the light-out transition.

    Words to learn

    mothnightsoftwingslampflutter

    Say this to your child

    “"A moth! Soft little wings — this friend wakes up at night, when we are tucked up. See how it flutters round the lamp? We watch from our window — outside light on, window shut. Flutter, flutter, go the moth wings. Sleep well, little moth!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say moth — then stroke your own arm gently: soft, soft, like the wings on the card.
    2. Flutter together: arms as soft wings, bumping gently around the room, landing on cushions — moths are the world’s clumsiest, loveliest flyers.
    3. Tell the night story: when toddlers go to bed, the moths wake up and visit the lamps — the garden has an evening crew.
    4. On a warm evening, stand together at the window with the outside light on and watch: is anyone fluttering out there? Maybe, maybe not — the waiting is the game.
    5. End with the rule, whispered for bedtime: moths are watch-from-inside friends. Wings stay soft, windows stay shut, and our eyes do the visiting.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say moth together and find the soft wings on the card — this one is brown and gentle-looking. Ask your toddler to flutter their arms once, then rest them wide like a moth having a daytime sleep.

    Ask your child

    "When does the moth wake up?" "What does it love — lamps, or soup?" "Can you flutter softly?" "Do we open the window to touch it, or watch from inside?" — answered with a flutter, a giggle and a firm little head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Moth night-night!" reported from the cot, soft-arm flutters adopted as a wind-down move, and moths announced at every lamppost and lit window — the night crew now has a name and a fan club.

    Out in the real world

    Moths gather at porch lights, lit windows and lamp posts on warm evenings — visible from indoors better than anywhere. Each flutter is a rerun: lights on, window shut, watch, wave goodnight.

    Try it together

    Porch-light vigil: five minutes at the window with the outside light on, whisper-counting any flutter that appears. No moths tonight? The game still worked — five quiet minutes of watching is its own bedtime magic.

    Understanding check

    At bedtime, ask who wakes up when we sleep: a confident moth means the day-night idea landed — the garden kept working in your toddler’s imagination all night long.

    Parent tips

    Keep the window closed and the watching brief; five minutes is the whole show at two. If a moth gets indoors, a grown-up can cup it in a glass and release it outside — narrate the rescue; it is excellent material.

    Staying safe

    The vigil happens from inside with the window shut, and moths are never caught — fingers rub the dust-fine powder off their wings and squeeze far more than anyone means to. Warm-evening lamp-watching stays on the indoors side, with a grown-up alongside.

    This lesson pairs with the Moth flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Cricket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches with ears instead of eyes: your toddler hears the cricket’s chirp on the card’s behalf, goes quiet on the doorstep on a warm evening, and plays the set’s best detective game — finding the singer without ever needing to.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A cricket is a small hopping insect that sings on summer evenings by rubbing its wings together — chirp, chirp, chirp. The song says the day is cooling down, and the singer hides beautifully in the grass.

    What does it mean?

    The cricket is the set’s sound-first card: the word arrives through the ears, and the eyes may never get a turn. That is a genuine milestone — listening on purpose, with a whole body gone still to help.

    What does the child need to know?

    Crickets chirp on warm evenings and hide in the grass, and finding them is a bonus, never the goal. The game is the listening: ears open, bodies quiet, song enjoyed — the musician stays hidden and unbothered.

    Why this matters

    Deliberate listening is the foundation under every later skill — words, music, reading. The cricket makes it a treasure hunt for sound, and the doorstep version doubles as the gentlest last-game-before-bed in the set.

    What it teaches

    Focused listening (ears leading, eyes helping), sound imitation, stillness as a listening tool, and evening vocabulary — cool, quiet, song — that softens the whole end of day.

    Words to learn

    cricketchirplistenquieteveningsong

    Say this to your child

    “"Listen... chirp, chirp, chirp! A cricket is singing somewhere in the grass. Can you hear it? Let’s be very quiet and listen with our ears. Can you make the cricket sound too? The cricket sings all evening — and we listen like little detectives."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say cricket — then make the sound together: chirp, chirp, chirp, as fast or slow as your fingers can go.
    2. Play the singer game: one of you closes their eyes while the other chirps from somewhere in the room — can the listener point to the song?
    3. Make a cricket of your own: run a fingertip slowly along a comb, or rub two sticks gently — there, that is the cricket’s own instrument.
    4. On a warm evening, sit together on the doorstep and go very quiet: ears up! Is the cricket singing tonight?
    5. End with the rule of the game: we listen, we whisper, and we let the singer stay hidden — crickets are heard-and-loved friends.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say cricket together and give the card a chirp, chirp. This cricket looks like it is singing — ask your toddler to make the chirping sound back, then go completely still and listen for a pretend answer.

    Ask your child

    "What does the cricket say?" "Can you hear the song?" "Where is the cricket hiding?" "Do we dig for the singer, or listen?" — answered with chirps, a cupped ear and a whispered hiding-in-the-grass.

    What your child can say or do

    "Chirp chirp!" hummed at bathtime and bedtime, sudden hushes on the doorstep with one finger raised — the family’s new signal for listening — and crickets credited with every evening sound from now on.

    Out in the real world

    Warm evenings bring the song to gardens, parks and any grassy verge — heard from prams, windows and doorsteps. Each chirp is a rerun: stop, hush, listen together, and walk on without needing to see the star of the show.

    Try it together

    Doorstep listening minute: one quiet minute on the step or at the open window, collecting every sound you hear — bird, car, cricket? — whispered back and forth. The cricket version of a bedtime wind-down.

    Understanding check

    On the next warm evening, watch the body when the song starts: if your toddler freezes into their listening pose without being asked, the ears learned the lesson — the quietest victory in the set.

    Parent tips

    Model the hush yourself; the listening pose is contagious. If the comb is fiddly, two fingers rubbed on a table edge work fine — the point is making the sound, not mastering the tool.

    Staying safe

    Doorstep and window listening stays with a grown-up and well back from steps and roads. No grass-parting or stone-turning to find the singer — hidden means hidden, and the song comes to you anyway.

    This lesson pairs with the Cricket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Roly Poly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rolls with the garden’s smallest gymnast: your toddler curls into a ball and unrolls slowly like the roly-poly on the card, then learns how the real ones get found — gently, under a pot, with the roof going back on.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A roly-poly is a small grey creature that rolls into a perfect round ball when it feels shy, then unrolls and trundles off on tiny legs. It lives in damp, dark corners — under pots, stones and leaves.

    What does it mean?

    Curl-and-unroll is the whole lesson in one body move: in, out, in, out. The roly-poly is also the friendliest-looking bug on the card, which makes it the perfect face for the garden’s look-don’t-poke rule.

    What does the child need to know?

    Roly-polies curl into balls and live under pots and stones, and they are look-don’t-poke friends: grown-up lifts, toddler looks, and the roof goes back gently. Hands get washed after every dark-corner adventure.

    Why this matters

    The curling game is real body control — tucking, balancing, holding a shape — and the pot-peeking rules rehearse patience and kindness at the same time. Small creature, enormous manners curriculum.

    What it teaches

    Body shaping and control (a tight ball is genuinely hard work), gentle curiosity, turn-taking in the peeking game, and the washing-hands routine that follows all soil play.

    Words to learn

    roly-polycurlballrollgentlegrey

    Say this to your child

    “"A roly-poly! Grey and tiny — and when it feels shy, it rolls into a little ball! Can you make yourself tiny and round, like it does? Tuck in tight... now unroll, slowly, slowly. We find them under pots with a grown-up — we look with our eyes and put the roof back."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say roly-poly — it is a funny name, so say it twice and enjoy the wobble of it.
    2. Curl up on the rug into the tiniest ball you can, then unroll slowly, one limb at a time — again! Again!
    3. Roll gently across the rug like a roly-poly trundling home, then curl back up at the far cushion.
    4. Tell the finding story: real roly-polies hide under pots and stones. Grown-up lifts, we peek with quiet eyes, and back goes the roof so our friend stays cosy.
    5. End with the routine: after peeking in dark corners, we wash our hands — and the roly-poly keeps its ball shape for another day.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say roly-poly together and look for the grey little bug on the card. Curl up small like it, hold the ball for three seconds, then unroll and ask if your toddler can make themselves just as round.

    Ask your child

    "What does the roly-poly do when it feels shy?" "Can you curl into a ball?" "Who lifts the pot?" "What do we do with our hands afterwards?" — answered with a curl, a point at you and a run to the tap.

    What your child can say or do

    "Again! Again!" between every curl and unroll, roly-polies requested by name at every flowerpot, and ball-shape freezing adopted anywhere a hug of courage is needed — the tiniest card doing the biggest body work.

    Out in the real world

    Roly-polies wait under pots, stones and damp leaves all year round. Each find is a rerun: grown-up lifts, one gentle look, a whispered roly-poly, and the roof lowered softly before small feet move on.

    Try it together

    Curl-and-unroll dice: call curl! and your toddler tucks into a ball; call unroll! and they unwind one arm at a time. Add roly-poly! for a gentle roll across the rug. Three commands, endless repeats.

    Understanding check

    Find a real roly-poly and watch the hands: if they stay down while the eyes go wide, the rule took — and if the pot gets patted goodbye, the kindness took as well.

    Parent tips

    Keep pot-peeks to one or two per session and let your toddler narrate what they saw afterwards — retelling is the learning. If no real roly-poly turns up, the curling game carries the card perfectly on its own.

    Staying safe

    Peeking under pots and stones is grown-up-hands work only — fingers stay out from underneath anything lifted. After dark-corner and soil play, hands get washed before snacks, and nothing from the garden goes in mouths.

    This lesson pairs with the Roly Poly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Firefly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is pure glow: your toddler learns the firefly’s blink, plays on-and-off with lights at home, and — if the season and the street allow — watches a dark garden window for the real thing, hands and windows safely still.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A firefly is a small beetle that can light up its own body, blinking on and off in the warm dark of summer evenings. The blinking is how fireflies chat with one another, and most toddlers meet them in books first.

    What does it mean?

    The firefly owns the set’s rarest word: glow. On-and-off is a toddler’s favourite game pattern — switches, torches, blinks — and here it arrives attached to a living thing that does it all by itself.

    What does the child need to know?

    Fireflies glow and blink at night, and they are watch-from-the-window friends: catching a firefly switches its light off, so eyes do the admiring and hands stay folded. The blinking games at home use torches and paper, not bugs.

    Why this matters

    Blink-and-freeze games teach watching and waiting in the dark — a big, brave skill at two. The deeper gift is wonder with patience attached: the real light comes on its own schedule, or not at all, and that is part of the magic.

    What it teaches

    On-off cause and effect, brave-and-calm darkness habits, watching patience at a dark window, and the idea that animals have their own language — light language, in this case.

    Words to learn

    fireflyglowblinknightlightdark

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — a firefly! A tiny light in the dark. Blink... blink... it talks with its light! Can you blink like a firefly? At night, we watch from the window with quiet eyes. The firefly keeps its glow, and we keep our hands to ourselves."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say firefly — then blink your hands: fingers open, fingers closed, the firefly’s own on-and-off.
    2. Play blink together in a dim room: light on, light off, whisper glow each time it comes back — the returning light is the joke.
    3. Craft a paper firefly and tuck a small torch or glow dot behind it, then let your toddler work the blinks: on... off... on...
    4. On a real summer night, stand at a dark window or garden step with a grown-up and watch: any tiny lights blinking out there? Quiet eyes, folded hands.
    5. End with the rule, whispered: fireflies are watch-only friends — their light stays on them, and our hands stay in ours.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say firefly together and find the light on the card — this firefly glows. Blink your hands open and closed like the firefly’s light, then ask your toddler to make their fingers glow too.

    Ask your child

    "What does the firefly do at night?" "Can you blink like a firefly?" "Where do we watch from — the window, or the garden?" "Do we catch the light, or look at it?" — answered with blinks, a point to the window and folded hands.

    What your child can say or do

    Hand-blinks in dim rooms at bedtime, fireflies announced at every streetlight and car light from now on, and glow whispered at any small light in the dark — the set’s quietest word, adopted overnight.

    Out in the real world

    Fireflies blink over summer lawns, parks and hedgerows in the right season and region — and every torch, phone flash and fairy light makes a fine stand-in the rest of the year. Each blink is a rerun: hush, watch, wave the light goodnight.

    Try it together

    Firefly torch game: in a dim room, your toddler is the firefly with a small torch — blink on, blink off, while you follow the light with your eyes only. Swap roles: now you glow, and they whisper glow each time.

    Understanding check

    Dim the lights tonight and start blinking: if your toddler joins in with glow on their lips, the card came alive — the light language landed exactly as written.

    Parent tips

    Keep the dark-watching short, warm and hand-held; bravery grows best in small doses. Any summer-evening garden watching happens with a grown-up, well away from steps, ponds and paths.

    Staying safe

    Dark-window and garden-step watching is a grown-up-and-toddler affair, hands linked, away from edges and water. Fireflies are never caught — jars and hands switch their lights off for good, so the watching is eyes-only, always.

    This lesson pairs with the Firefly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Praying Mantis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson stands very still and wins: your toddler folds their arms like the mantis on the card, holds the pose one breath longer than seems possible, and meets the garden’s quietest hunter — admired from afar, arms and all.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A praying mantis is a tall green insect that stands up on long legs and holds its front arms folded, as if saying hello or thinking hard. It waits without moving for a very long time — then catches its dinner in one quick snap.

    What does it mean?

    The mantis is the stillness card: every other bug teaches a movement, and this one teaches the absence of it. Toddlers adore a challenge, and stand-still-longer-than-you is the set’s finest quiet contest.

    What does the child need to know?

    The mantis stands tall with folded arms and waits patiently, and those clever front legs catch bugs — which is exactly why they stay far away from fingers. Watching a real one means standing just as patiently, a little way back.

    Why this matters

    Holding still on purpose is real self-regulation, and the mantis gives it a hero: a whole animal whose superpower is waiting. The folded arms make the pose copyable, and the quiet makes it a lovely wind-down game.

    What it teaches

    Stillness and balance as skills in their own right, body imitation (the fold is genuinely tricky), patience with a living model, and the keep-your-distance rule for hunters of any size.

    Words to learn

    mantisstillarmswaitgreengentle

    Say this to your child

    “"A praying mantis! See how it stands — arms folded, perfectly still. Can you stand like it? Fold your arms... shhh... hold it... The mantis waits and waits, then catches its dinner. We watch with quiet eyes and our hands stay way back."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say praying mantis — then fold your arms up like the card: hello, says the mantis, very politely and very still.
    2. Play the copy game: fold arms, stand tall, hold it... and hold it... until somebody giggles. The giggler folds again.
    3. Try the stillness record: how many breaths can the whole family hold the mantis pose? Count them out loud, slowly.
    4. Tell the waiting story: the mantis stands still because it is waiting for its dinner to walk past — patience is its superpower.
    5. End with the rule, quietly: the mantis catches bugs with those front arms, so our fingers stay far away — we watch, we fold our own arms, and we admire.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say praying mantis together and spot the folded arms on the card — this one is green and standing tall. Make the mantis pose yourself, then ask your toddler to hold it while you count slowly to three.

    Ask your child

    "What are the mantis’s arms doing?" "Can you stand still like the mantis?" "What is it waiting for?" "Do our fingers go near the mantis’s arms, or stay back?" — answered with a fold, a hush and careful little steps backwards.

    What your child can say or do

    Arms folded at the dinner table with tremendous dignity, stillness contests instigated against parents and pets, and mantises announced in every tall plant — the garden’s statue has a fan who now stands just as quietly.

    Out in the real world

    Mantises perch on stems, hedges and flower heads, standing so still they are easy to miss and marvellous to find. Each sighting is a rerun: spot it, fold arms, admire the stillness, and step back kindly.

    Try it together

    Mantis statues: dance gently around the room until someone calls mantis! — then freeze in the folded-arms pose, tallest and stillest wins. Add a slow breath at the end; even statues need to breathe.

    Understanding check

    Call the mantis pose at a random moment tomorrow: a frozen, folded, solemn toddler means the card landed — patience arrived on six long legs, and it can be summoned on request.

    Parent tips

    Join every contest and lose some on purpose — being beaten at stillness by a two-year-old is the funniest, most motivating prize going. Keep the front-leg rule light; a warning said calmly lands better than one said in alarm.

    Staying safe

    A mantis catches its food with spiky front arms and one quick snap, so real ones are watched from a respectful distance with hands well back. The folded-arms game stays on rugs and grass — statues and hard floors do not mix.

    This lesson pairs with the Praying Mantis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Centipede — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson walks on a hundred make-believe legs: your toddler learns the centipede’s rippling walk with ten wiggly fingers, counts legs until counting collapses into giggles, and meets the quickest mover in the garden’s dark corners.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A centipede is a long, flat creature with very, very many legs that ripple along in waves, carrying it surprisingly fast over the ground. It likes dark, damp places and hurries out of the light.

    What does it mean?

    The centipede is the set’s exaggeration card: no toddler will ever count its real legs, and that is the fun — enormous numbers become a joke, a wiggle and a race rather than a lesson.

    What does the child need to know?

    Centipedes have many legs and hurry through dark, damp corners, and they are look-don’t-touch friends like the rest of the set. After any under-the-pot adventure, the sink comes next.

    Why this matters

    Finger-walking builds the little muscles that later hold crayons, and the leg-counting silliness keeps numbers playful exactly when they start getting big. The hurry-away habit also explains something useful: dark corners belong to the creatures in them.

    What it teaches

    Fine-motor wiggles (ten fingers, independent legs), big-number silliness, observation of fast small movers, and the after-soil hand-washing routine, rehearsed again.

    Words to learn

    centipedelegswigglefastdarkcount

    Say this to your child

    “"A centipede! One leg, two legs... SO many legs! See them ripple — wiggle, wiggle, off it goes! Can your fingers walk like a centipede? Fast, fast! Centipedes love dark corners, so we peek with our eyes only — and wash our hands after the garden."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say centipede — then count a few legs out loud, give up happily, and declare: SO many legs!
    2. Walk your fingers across the table like a centipede — wiggling, rippling, off somewhere in a rush — and let your toddler’s fingers race yours.
    3. Be centipedes on the rug: crawl on hands and knees with extra-fast wiggles, then freeze when the light comes on — centipedes dash for the dark.
    4. Tell the hiding story: centipedes adore dark, damp corners, so under pots and logs is where they hurry home to.
    5. End with the rule: many-legged friends are look-at friends — eyes follow, fingers stay, and hands get washed after every garden adventure.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say centipede together and find the legs on the card — this one is long, with many legs to point at. Count two or three of them, then walk your fingers along the card like a tiny many-legged friend.

    Ask your child

    "How many legs does the centipede have?" "Can your fingers walk like it?" "Where do centipedes like to hide?" "Do we touch the many-legged friend, or watch?" — answered with wiggles, a big number guess and pointing fingers only.

    What your child can say or do

    Finger-centipedes racing across every table and tummy, absurd leg-counts shouted with total confidence — one hundred! — and centipedes spotted at every log and flowerpot, always off somewhere at speed.

    Out in the real world

    Centipedes dash through gardens, under logs and along damp walls, most often seen as a fast ripple and then gone. Each glimpse is a rerun: point, whisper centipede, watch it hurry, and let it get where it was going.

    Try it together

    Finger-leg races: two centipedes (one hand each, or two for the advanced) race across a table from edge to edge. Fast wiggles, slow wiggles, backwards wiggles — the legs decide everything.

    Understanding check

    Ask tomorrow how many legs a centipede has: any enormous, delighted number is a perfect pass — the exaggeration landed, and so did the wiggle that carries it.

    Parent tips

    Keep the counting brief and the wiggle long; the race teaches more than the arithmetic at this age. If a real centipede startles you, borrow its own lesson — freeze, breathe, and narrate it hurrying home.

    Staying safe

    Centipedes hurry away rather than hug, but fingers stay out of dark corners all the same — pot-lifting is grown-up work, and peeking is eyes-only. Garden play ends at the sink: hands washed, snacks after, nothing from the garden in mouths.

    This lesson pairs with the Centipede flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Earthworm — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson honours the garden’s hidden hero: your toddler wiggles like the pink earthworm on the card, rolls worms out of playdough, and learns why the busiest hands in the soil are the ones we never touch.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    An earthworm is a long, soft, pink creature that lives in the soil, wiggling through it all day and turning old leaves into food for plants. No worm, no garden — they are the quiet workers beneath every bloom your toddler has ever sniffed.

    What does it mean?

    The earthworm is the set’s least glamorous card and its deepest lesson: the most important worker is the one nobody sees. For a two-year-old, the worm is also the perfect wiggle — long, slow, and impossible to do standing up.

    What does the child need to know?

    Worms wiggle underground and come up after rain, and they are never-touch friends: their skin does their breathing, and dry hands would hurt it. We watch with kind eyes, and if one is stranded on the path, a grown-up moves it with a leaf.

    Why this matters

    Caring for a creature too small and soft to defend itself is kindness at its purest — and the reason is touchable: worm skin breathes, so our dry hands are the danger. Rules with real reasons stick for life.

    What it teaches

    Long, slow body wiggles (surprisingly hard, endlessly funny), the underground-world idea, gentleness practised at its most delicate, and rain-day observation habits.

    Words to learn

    earthwormwigglesoilrainsoftkind

    Say this to your child

    “"An earthworm! Pink and wiggly — it lives under the ground and helps the flowers grow. Wiggle, wiggle! After rain it comes up to breathe. We watch with our kind eyes and never touch — our hands are too dry, and the worm is very soft."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say earthworm — then wiggle: arms loose, shoulders loose, everything wiggling like something with no bones at all.
    2. Lie on the rug and do the worm: stretch long, pull in short, stretch long again — travelling by wiggles only.
    3. Roll playdough worms together — long, longer, the longest worm in the garden — and line them up for a wiggle parade.
    4. After rain, look for a real worm on a path or lawn and watch how it reaches and bunches, stretch by stretch: it came up for air, like a little swimmer.
    5. End with the rule, softly: a worm’s skin does its breathing, so our dry hands stay far away — we watch, we wiggle like them, and we leave them to their rain.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say earthworm together and look for the pink wiggler on the card. Ask your toddler to wiggle like the worm, then trace its long body with one finger from end to end and back again.

    Ask your child

    "Where does the worm live?" "When does it come up — after what?" "Can you wiggle like a worm?" "Do our hands touch the worm, or stay dry and far away?" — answered with wiggles, the word rain and a gentle head-shake.

    What your child can say or do

    "Wiggle worm!" announced at bathtime and every rainy window, playdough worms coiled all over the kitchen table, and worms rescued-in-story after every shower of rain — the underground hero has a spokesman.

    Out in the real world

    Rainy days bring worms up onto paths and lawns, and every one is a rerun: crouch, whisper earthworm, watch it stretch, and leave it to its air. Dry-weather digging turns up another — admired, then left to its tunnel.

    Try it together

    Playdough worm families: roll a mummy worm, a baby worm and the longest worm of all, then measure them against each other and against a real finger. Quiet hands, soft dough, and the worm’s whole shape lesson in one sitting.

    Understanding check

    Next rainy day, watch the crouch: if your toddler leans in to look with hands clasped behind their back, the rule grew roots — kindness and knowing, exactly as planted.

    Parent tips

    The never-touch rule needs its reason said out loud at least once: worm skin breathes, and our dry hands would hurt it. Reasons turn rules into values — and this one is true.

    Staying safe

    Worms are watched, never handled — even gently, dry fingers damage their skin. After rain or soil play, hands get washed before anything touches a face or snack, and nothing from the garden goes in mouths, ever.

    This lesson pairs with the Earthworm flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bird — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson looks up: your toddler learns the word bird, makes the tweet, and meets the garden’s fastest visitor — the friend that only comes close when everyone gets very quiet and very still.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A bird is an animal with feathers and wings that flies, hops and sings. This one is a bluebird perched on a branch — and birds like it visit gardens, hedges and windowsills every single morning, hunting seeds and crumbs.

    What does it mean?

    Birds are the only wild animals most toddlers see every day, doing exactly what toddlers love: appearing, moving, disappearing. Naming the bird turns the window into a daily show with a returning cast.

    What does the child need to know?

    Birds tweet, fly and hop, and they come to stillness: running feet send them off, quiet feet bring them near. We watch birds and never chase — the stiller the watcher, the longer the show.

    Why this matters

    Bird-watching is patience with a payoff — the child sees, in minutes, that quiet bodies are rewarded. That cause and effect is learned in the body, and it transfers to every library, queue and waiting room to come.

    What it teaches

    Stillness as a real skill, sound imitation, visual tracking of the quickest thing in the garden, and the gentle beginnings of caring about wild things that need nothing from us.

    Words to learn

    birdtweetwingsseedsquietfly

    Say this to your child

    “"Listen — tweet tweet! A bird! Birds have wings and they fly, and they hop along the fence. Let’s be quiet as mice and watch the window... still feet, soft voices... maybe a bird will come and say hello. Birds are our look-at friends!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say bird — then tweet together, two little songs, so the word arrives with its sound.
    2. Find the bird’s parts on the card: the wing, the beak, the tail, the branch it sits on — pointing is how two-year-olds read a picture.
    3. Take the card to the window and whisper: is a bird out there right now? Look quietly. A pigeon counts, a crow counts, everything with wings counts.
    4. Sprinkle a few seeds on a sill or step, step back, and hold the stillness together — count the quiet seconds out loud, softly.
    5. End with the rule: birds are watch-friends — quiet feet, down-held hands, and they come close all by themselves.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say bird together and point out the bluebird — on this card it sits on a branch. Point to the branch, then the wing, then tweet twice, softly, so the card stays a window game and not a shout.

    Ask your child

    "What does the bird say?" "Where is the bird sitting?" "Can you make your feet go still?" "Do we chase the bird, or watch it?" — answered with a tweet, a point and feet that stop on request.

    What your child can say or do

    "Bird!" shouted at full outdoor volume and whispered at indoor windows, tweets exchanged over breakfast, and every pigeon, crow and duck promoted to the same beloved word — the sky is officially inhabited now.

    Out in the real world

    Birds are the most reliable show in any street: fences, hedges, car parks, washing lines. Each visit is a rerun — point, whisper, watch, wave goodbye — and the seeds keep the cast coming back.

    Try it together

    Seed sprinkle and freeze: shake a tiny cup of seeds onto a step or sill, then hold hands and play freeze — crouch, breathe loud enough to hear, wait. The prize for winning is usually a bird.

    Understanding check

    At the next window, watch the feet and the voice: still feet and a whisper mean the lesson landed — your toddler has traded chasing for watching, which is the whole trade this card offers.

    Parent tips

    Keep a card and a seed cup by the window permanently; the ritual runs itself within a week. Two minutes is a full sitting at this age — stop while the pointing is still happy.

    Staying safe

    Windows and doors stay shut during bird-watching, and sills are for seeds, not elbows. Feed birds outside where they stay wild, wash little hands after touching seed, and let the chasing happen only in games.

    This lesson pairs with the Bird flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Frog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns your rug into a pond: your toddler learns the frog’s crouch and leap, ribbits between landings, and absorbs the set’s water rule — real frogs live at ponds, and ponds are grown-up-hand places.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A frog is a small, green, long-legged animal that sits still by the water and then disappears in a single huge leap. It catches bugs with a quick flick of its tongue and says — everyone together — ribbit.

    What does it mean?

    The frog is the set’s movement finale: crouch, launch, land, repeat. And because real frogs live at the water’s edge, the card doubles as the gentlest water-safety lesson in the garden.

    What does the child need to know?

    Frogs crouch and leap and say ribbit, and they live by ponds. We look at frogs from the bank — their damp skin is far too delicate for warm, dry hands — and any real pond means a grown-up holds on.

    Why this matters

    Jumping builds the big power skills — crouch depth, launch, controlled landing — while the pond rule rehearses respect for wild skin and water. One card, two lessons, both learned in the legs.

    What it teaches

    Explosive jumping and quiet landing, listening-freeze control, amphibian vocabulary, and water-safety habits rehearsed long before any real pond is in sight.

    Words to learn

    frogjumpribbitpondlily padgentle

    Say this to your child

    “"A frog! Ribbit, ribbit! Frogs crouch down low... and JUMP! Can you leap to the lily pad? Frogs live by the pond — when we visit, we hold hands and watch from the bank. We never pick frogs up; their skin is soft and ours is too dry. Ribbit!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say frog — then crouch low yourself, hands between your knees: the shape teaches before the word lands.
    2. Do one enormous jump together and land with a soft plop, then say ribbit! Word, jump and sound in one event.
    3. Scatter cushions as lily pads and leap from pad to pad, ribbiting on every landing — the quieter the landing, the better the frog.
    4. Tell the pond story simply: real frogs sit by the water, and we visit ponds holding a grown-up’s hand — we look from the bank, and our hands stay in ours.
    5. Finish with the still frog: crouch very small and freeze — then one last giant leap to end the session on a laugh.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say frog together and spot the green one waiting on the card. Crouch like the frog, hold for one breath, then leap once on the spot and give your biggest ribbit as you land.

    Ask your child

    "What does the frog say?" "Can you leap like a frog?" "Where do frogs live?" "Do we touch the frog at the pond, or watch from the bank?" — answered with a ribbit, a leap and a solemn linked-hands gesture.

    What your child can say or do

    "Ribbit!" punctuating bath time, cushion ponds rebuilt daily across the living room, and frogs announced at every puddle and pond on every walk — with feet stopping at the bank, which is the rule arriving.

    Out in the real world

    Frogs appear at pond edges, damp gardens and after-rain paths — mostly as a flash of green and a splash. Each flash is a rerun: freeze, whisper frog, watch the jump, and keep feet on dry land.

    Try it together

    Lily-pad hop course: cushions spaced across the rug, frog crouch between each leap, silent-landing points awarded generously. End as every good frog does — one enormous final jump into your arms.

    Understanding check

    Say ribbit out of nowhere tomorrow: if a crouch-jump arrives before the laugh does, the word lives in the legs — the pond rule usually arrives in the same package, so listen for the bank part too.

    Parent tips

    Join every leap; your landing quality sets the standard. Keep pond talk warm and frequent — baths, paddling pools, puddles — because water rules work best when they are rehearsed everywhere, not just at ponds.

    Staying safe

    Real ponds, streams and even deep puddles are grown-up-hand territory, always. Frogs are never picked up — their damp skin is delicate and would dry out on ours — so the leaping stays on cushions and the watching stays on the bank.

    This lesson pairs with the Frog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN BUGS & FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Squirrel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson borrows the garden’s quickest game: your toddler scurries and freezes like the squirrel on the card, plays the nut-hiding trick that real squirrels play all winter, and learns to watch the park’s best show from the path.

    Download the card ↓

    How to use this card

    What is this?

    A squirrel is a quick, bushy-tailed animal that runs up trees, along fences and across lawns, burying nuts to find again later. Its tail flicks and twitches — and it is almost always the first wild animal a toddler meets doing something dramatic.

    What does it mean?

    Squirrels close the set with the game toddlers were born for: dash, stop, look. The nut-burying story gives the dash a plot, and the tail gives the whole animal a flag your child will spot from a pram at fifty paces.

    What does the child need to know?

    Squirrels scurry, freeze and flick their fluffy tails, and they are watch-from-the-path friends: wild things stay wild, so we never chase, touch or feed them — admiring is the better gift.

    Why this matters

    Freeze-and-watch is attention training disguised as the squirrel’s own trick, and spotting one in a tree is a genuine search-and-find triumph. Owning an animal seen every day builds the confident feeling that the world is knowable.

    What it teaches

    Visual tracking at top speed, impulse control (the freeze), pretend play with a plot (bury, remember, dig), and respect for wild animals met on their own terms.

    Words to learn

    squirreltailtreenutsscurrywatch

    Say this to your child

    “"A squirrel! See the big fluffy tail — twitch, twitch! Squirrels run up trees and bury their nuts for winter. Can you scurry like a squirrel? Now freeze — and look around! When we see a real one, we stand on the path and watch its show. No chasing, no feeding — just watching."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say squirrel — then wag an arm-tail behind you: the make-believe tail makes the word unforgettable.
    2. Play the squirrel’s own game: scurry three steps, freeze, look left, look right, scurry again — narrating every move as you both do it.
    3. Hide a toy nut under one of three cups, shuffle slowly, and let your squirrel find it — then swap: you hunt, they hide.
    4. Tell the winter story: squirrels bury nuts everywhere and come back for them later — some are forgotten, and those grow into trees.
    5. End with the rule, on the move: squirrels are watch-from-the-path friends — eyes follow, feet stay with the grown-up, and hands stay full of nothing.

    Look closer at the picture

    Say squirrel together and find the tail on the card — this one has a big fluffy tail. Wag your arm-tail while you ask what the tail is doing, then scurry-and-freeze once across the rug.

    Ask your child

    "What is the squirrel’s tail doing?" "Where does the squirrel run — up what?" "Where did it put the nuts?" "Do we chase the squirrel, or watch from the path?" — answered with a wag, a point upwards and still little feet.

    What your child can say or do

    "Squirrel!" announced at top volume in every park and garden, arm-tails wagged at dinner, nut-hiding games running under sofas all winter — and the first honest freeze when a real one dashes past, the watching rule working exactly as built.

    Out in the real world

    Squirrels perform daily wherever trees grow: gardens, parks, churchyards, the tree outside the bakery. Every dash is a rerun — point, whisper, follow with your eyes, and keep your feet on the path.

    Try it together

    Three-cup squirrel stash: hide a nut or a small toy under one cup, shuffle, and let your squirrel remember where it went. Squirrels lose a few nuts every winter too — losing the round is part of the joke.

    Understanding check

    On the next walk, watch the feet when a real squirrel appears: still, or running? Still feet and a pointing finger mean the lesson landed — the freeze replaced the chase, and the show got a respectful audience.

    Parent tips

    Say eyes follow, feet stay on every sighting until your toddler finishes the line for you. Keep the cup game tiny — three cups, one treasure — and let your child be the hider half the time; hiding is the cleverer job.

    Staying safe

    Squirrels are wild things with tiny sharp teeth and quicker claws, so watching happens from the path with hands down — no chasing, no offering food, and no collecting acorns or conkers for anything but the toy game. Hands get washed after conker play, and nothing from the park goes in mouths.

    This lesson pairs with the Squirrel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Bugs & Friends (Toddler 8).
